title: Seeds & Germination
hook: A seed is a tiny plant on pause — a packed embryo with a lunch box of food, waiting for the right moment to wake up and push into the world.
key_points: A seed holds a plant embryo, a food store, and a protective coat.
Seeds can stay dormant for months or years until conditions are right.
Germination — sprouting — usually needs water, oxygen, and the right temperature.
The root emerges first to anchor and drink, then a shoot reaches for light.
content_html: A seed looks lifeless, but it's really a plant on pause. Inside its protective coat sits a tiny embryo — a baby plant — alongside a built-in food supply to power its first burst of growth. That packaging lets a seed survive harsh conditions and wait, sometimes for years, until the timing is right.
extra_html: Germination is the moment a seed wakes up and starts to grow. Most seeds need three things to trigger it: water to swell and soften the seed, oxygen to fuel the embryo's metabolism, and a temperature that signals a favorable season. When those line up, the embryo springs into action. The root, or radicle, usually emerges first, pushing downward to anchor the seedling and pull in water, before a shoot rises toward sunlight to begin photosynthesis. As Encyclopaedia Britannica describes, this dormancy-then-sprouting strategy is one of the great advantages of seed plants — it lets them spread their offspring across time as well as space.

related.title: How Plants Reproduce
related.hook: Flowers aren't just decoration — they're how most plants have sex, trading pollen so they can pack the next generation into seeds that travel.

related.title: How a Plant Is Built
related.hook: Most plants are made of three working parts — roots that drink, stems that lift, and leaves that catch sunlight — and together they turn dirt and light into a living thing.

flashcards.prompt: What are the three main parts packed inside a seed?
flashcards.back_html: A plant embryo (the baby plant), a food store to fuel its first growth, and a tough seed coat that protects it until conditions are right.

flashcards.prompt: What does germination usually require to begin?

choices.text: Water, oxygen, and a suitable temperature
A pollinator to visit the seed

flashcards.explanation_html: A dormant seed stays asleep until it senses the right cues — typically moisture, air, and warmth — which signal that it's safe to sprout.

flashcards.prompt: When a seed germinates, which part typically emerges first?

choices.text: The root, which anchors the seedling and takes up water
A flower, ready to make new seeds
A fruit full of more seeds

flashcards.explanation_html: The root comes out first to grip the soil and draw in water, before the shoot pushes upward toward the light.
